“I examined the skull drawing carefully. Its outer lines, the ones closest to the edge of the vellum, were much clearer than the rest. Obviously, the heat had worked incompletely or unevenly. I immediately lit a fire and held every part of the parchment close to its glowing heat. At first this merely darkened the skull’s faint lines. But as I continued, another shape appeared in the corner diagonally opposite the skull. At first I thought it was a goat. Looking more closely, however, I became certain that it was meant to be a kid.”

“Ha! Ha!” I said. “Of course I have no right to laugh at you—a million and a half in money is too serious to joke about. But you can’t add a third link to your chain this way. You won’t find any special connection between pirates and a goat. Pirates have nothing to do with goats, you know. Goats belong to farming.”

“But I just told you the picture wasn’t of a goat.”

“All right, a kid, then. Much the same thing.”

“Much the same, but not exactly,” said Legrand. “Perhaps you’ve heard of a certain Captain Kidd. I immediately took the animal to be a signature made as a visual pun, or a symbol standing for a name. I call it a signature because of its position on the vellum. In the same way, the skull in the diagonally opposite corner looked like a stamp or seal. What troubled me greatly was that nothing else appeared. The document I imagined had no body; I had the surrounding clues but no text.”

“I suppose you expected a letter between the stamp and the signature.”

“Something like that. The truth is, I had an overwhelming feeling that some enormous piece of good fortune was approaching. I can hardly explain why. Perhaps it was really a wish rather than a belief. But did you know that Jupiter’s foolish remark about the bug being solid gold had a remarkable effect on my imagination? Then there was the string of accidents and coincidences. They were so extraordinary. Do you see what sheer chance it was that all this happened on the only day of the entire year that had been, or might be, cold enough to need a fire? And that without the fire, or without the dog coming in at precisely that moment, I would never have discovered the skull, and therefore would never have come into possession of the treasure?”

For that reason, I determined to get down the moment we reached the town, and place myself beyond his hearing. I carried out this stratagem successfully. My small portmanteau lay in the boot beneath my feet; a turn of a hinge was all that was needed to release it. I tossed it down ahead of me, climbed down after it, and found myself beside the first lamp on the first paving-stones of the town. The convicts continued with the coach, and I knew where they would be whisked away to the river. In imagination I saw the boat and its convict crew waiting at the slime-washed steps, heard once more the harsh “Give way, you!” like a command addressed to dogs, and again saw that wicked Noah’s Ark resting on the dark water.

I could not have named the object of my fear, which was entirely vague and shapeless, but I was terribly afraid. Walking toward the hotel, I felt myself trembling with a dread far greater than the simple prospect of an unpleasant or painful recognition. I am certain that it assumed no definite form, and was merely, for a few minutes, the return of childhood’s terror.

The Blue Boar’s coffee-room was deserted. I had ordered dinner and even seated myself before it when the waiter recognized me. Having apologized for his lapse of memory, he asked whether he should send Boots to fetch Mr. Pumblechook.

“No,” I replied, “certainly not.”

The waiter—the same one who had delivered the Great Remonstrance from the Commercials on the day I was bound apprentice—seemed astonished. At his first opportunity he placed an old, grubby local newspaper so squarely before me that I picked it up and read the following paragraph:

Our readers will discover, not entirely without interest, concerning the recent romantic advancement in fortune of a youthful worker in iron from this vicinity (what a subject, incidentally, for the enchanted pen of our townsman TOOBY, the poet of these columns, whose recognition is not yet universal!), that his first patron, companion, and friend was a much-respected person not wholly unconnected with the trade in corn and seeds, whose exceptionally convenient and spacious business premises stand within a hundred miles of the High Street. It is not altogether apart from our private feelings that we name HIM as Mentor to our young Telemachus, since it is gratifying to know that our own town gave birth to the founder of the latter’s fortunes.

We insisted so loudly and desperately that we were free men that the speaker who kept talking about liberty, and his patriotic audience, began to take an interest. They crowded around us with a very determined air. The speaker said:

“If you really are free men, you have nothing to fear. Britain’s God-given liberties will shield and protect you! (Applause.) You shall soon see. Show us your proof.”

“What proof?”

“Proof that you are free men.”

Ah—I remembered! I came to my senses and said nothing. But the king burst out:

“You’re mad, man. It would make far more sense to demand that this thief and scoundrel prove we are not free men.”

You see, he understood his own laws as people so often do: he knew their words, not their effects. They acquire meaning, and become painfully clear, when they are applied to you.

Everyone shook their heads and looked disappointed. Some lost interest and turned away. The speaker spoke again, this time in a practical tone, with none of his earlier emotion:

“If you don’t know your country’s laws, it’s time you learned them. You are strangers to us; you cannot deny that. You may be free men; we do not deny that. But you may also be slaves. The law is clear. The man claiming you does not have to prove you are slaves. You must prove you are not.”

I said:

“Sir, please, just give us time to send a message to Astolat, or to the Valley of Holiness—”

“Quiet, good man. These are extraordinary requests, and you cannot expect them to be granted. They would take a great deal of time and cause your master unjustified inconvenience—”

“Master, you idiot!” the king roared. “I have no master. I myself am the m—”

“Be quiet, for God’s sake!”

I spoke just in time to stop him. We were in enough trouble already. Letting these people think we were mad would hardly improve our situation.

There is no point dragging out the details. The earl put us up for auction and sold us. The same devilish law existed in our own South during my lifetime, more than thirteen hundred years later. Hundreds of free men unable to prove their freedom had been sold into slavery for life under it, without making much impression on me. But the moment I personally encountered that law and the auction block, something I had merely considered wrong suddenly became hellish. Well, that is human nature.

Yes, they auctioned us like pigs. In a large town with a busy market we would have fetched a good price. But this place was utterly lifeless, and we sold for an amount that still makes me ashamed whenever I remember it.
